After more than two decades chasing the most violent explosions in the universe, NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has gone quiet. NASA announced October 23 that the spacecraft has concluded operations and is expected to re-enter Earth's atmosphere in the next few weeks, closing a mission designed to last two years that instead ran for more than 22.

Swift's end was written by the Sun. Increased solar activity heated and expanded Earth's upper atmosphere, increasing drag on the satellite until it began sinking rapidly. A high-risk, fast-turnaround servicing mission — a commercial spacecraft built in under a year to grab Swift and boost it to a higher orbit — ended in August without an attempt at the boost, after its own technical failures left it without enough fuel.

NASA then restarted Swift's science observations, which had been paused to minimize drag, and the observatory kept working until October 20, when it sank to 171 miles (275 kilometers) and could no longer compensate for the drag. It entered safe mode, and the operations team at Penn State sent the command that effectively ended the mission to prepare it for re-entry.

Swift's legacy is measured in speed. Launched November 20, 2004, from Cape Canaveral, it was built to solve a mystery more than three decades old: what causes gamma-ray bursts, the brief flashes of high-energy radiation that are the most powerful explosions known. Its ability to pivot to a new burst within about a minute turned those flashes from rumors that faded before anyone could look into laboratories, and its rapid alerts let telescopes on Earth and in orbit observe the same event almost immediately.

Most of the 1,450-kilogram spacecraft should burn up on re-entry, and NASA has published no debris assessment; the exact day and place remain unknown, depending on solar activity. Other telescopes will keep watching for gamma-ray bursts, but none combined Swift's rapid detection with its multi-wavelength view — a combination that defined time-domain astronomy for a generation.

  • Associated Press via Britannica, "Private spacecraft falls back to Earth after failing to rescue aging NASA telescope," September 25, 2026
